query: Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo is a disordered BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with a room-temperature compressive yield strength of 1719 MPa, but its high Mo content increases the electronegativity difference and is associated with reduced plasticity. What single intervention could improve its room-temperature compressive strength–plasticity balance without sacrificing its high strength? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, the operative mechanism, the predicted change in strength and plasticity relative to the equiatomic disordered-BCC alloy, the conditions and limits under which the effect should occur, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a trace amount of boron (~0.1 atomic percent) to the equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo disordered BCC alloy will enhance its room‐temperature compressive plasticity without compromising its high yield strength. The boron is expected to segregate to the grain boundaries, thereby improving grain‐boundary cohesion and delaying intergranular fracture initiated by the high electronegativity difference induced by Mo.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo disordered BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with a high compressive yield strength (~1719 MPa) but limited compressive ductility due to a high Mo content.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled, trace addition of boron (~0.1 at.%) during alloy melting and homogenization.
generation.conditions: The alloy will be produced via conventional arc melting under an inert atmosphere followed by homogenization and a cooling step optimized to promote boron segregation to grain boundaries. Room-temperature compressive tests will be conducted to compare the mechanical balance.
generation.structural_mediator: Boron atoms segregating to the grain boundaries reduce the local interfacial energy and enhance cohesion, thus mitigating premature grain‐boundary–mediated fracture while maintaining the bulk solid‐solution strengthening of the BCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: At low concentrations, boron acts as a beneficial interstitial element. It preferentially segregates to grain boundaries, reducing embrittlement associated with high local electronegativity differences from Mo. This improved cohesion at the grain boundaries raises the ductility by impeding crack initiation and propagation, while the main BCC matrix continues to deliver the high yield strength from Mo-based solid solution strengthening.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified alloy, the boron-doped alloy is expected to retain a yield strength near 1719 MPa while showing a significant increase in compressive strain to failure (e.g., from around 4–5% up to over 10%).
generation.baseline: The original equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo alloy without any boron addition exhibits very high yield strength but suffers from low compressive plasticity.
generation.boundary: This beneficial effect is expected at room temperature and within a narrow boron concentration range (likely below 0.5 at.%); higher boron contents could lead to the formation of brittle boride phases that would counteract the improvement in plasticity.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal boron content and its segregation behavior in refractory high-entropy alloys remain uncertain. This study builds on findings from interstitial carbon additions (as noted in PMC5227964 and PMC7514121) but introduces boron—a less explored dopant in this system—to specifically target grain-boundary cohesion. The exact quantitative effect on ductility and any interaction with the Mo-induced electronegativity difference need experimental verification.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractHigh-entropy alloys (HEAs) consisting of multiple principle elements provide an avenue for realizing exceptional mechanical, physical and chemical properties. We report a novel strategy for designing a new class of HEAs incorporating the additional interstitial element carbon. This results in joint activation of twinning- and transformation-induced plasticity (TWIP and TRIP) by tuning the matrix phase’s instability in a metastable TRIP-assisted dual-phase HEA. Besides TWIP and TRIP, such alloys benefit from massive substitutional and interstitial solid solution strengthening as well as from the composite effect associated with its dual-phase structure. Nanosize particle formation and grain size reduction are also utilized. The new interstitial TWIP-TRIP-HEA thus unifies all metallic strengthening mechanisms in one material, leading to twice the tensile strength compared to a single-phase HEA with similar composition, yet, at identical ductility.

AbstractNowadays refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are regarded as great candidates for the replacement of superalloys at high temperature. To design a RHEA, one must understand the pros and cons of every refractory element. However, the elemental effect on mechanical properties remains unclear. In this study, the subtraction method was applied on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys to discover the role of each element, and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were fabricated and analyzed. The microstructure and mechanical properties of each alloy at the as-cast state were examined. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solution strengthening effect are also discussed. Finally, the mechanism of how Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr affect the HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys was established after comparing the properties of these alloys.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, refractory high-entropy alloys, alloys design, elevated-temperature yield strength, solid solution strengthening effect
